summaries.example: Imagine two names for the same planet: one name is used when people see it in the evening, and another when they see it in the morning. If both names always point to that planet, the sentence “The two names point to the same planet” cannot become false just because the planet looks different. But “the brightest object in the evening sky” could point to another planet in a different situation, so that description is less fixed.
summaries.summary: A rigid designator is a word or phrase that refers to the same object whenever we imagine situations in which that object exists. Proper names are the clearest examples in the entry. A description such as “the brightest object in the evening sky” may refer to Venus now, but it could refer to Mars in a different possible situation. This difference helps explain why “Hesperus is Phosphorus”—two names for Venus—can be necessary if true, even though people had to use observation to discover it. The idea is also used in discussions of time, kinds such as water, properties, and the mind. Philosophers debate how broadly rigidity should apply and whether rival views, such as counterpart theory, describe what happens in other possible worlds more accurately.
key_ideas: Names are often treated as rigid: they keep referring to the same object when we imagine different ways things could have been.
Descriptions can be non-rigid because the thing fitting a description might change in another possible situation.
A statement can be discovered through experience but still be necessary if it uses two rigid names for the same object.
Philosophers disagree about whether words for kinds, properties, and expressions such as “you” are always rigid.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rigidity helps philosophers separate two questions: how we find out that something is true and how things could possibly be. It also gives them a tool for thinking about names, identity, scientific discoveries, and claims about what a person or thing could have been. The idea is useful, but its exact meaning and its application to kinds and properties remain debated.

important_terms.definition: A word or phrase used to pick out, or talk about, a particular thing.
A designator that picks out the same object in every possible situation where that object exists.
A way things could have been, different from how things actually are.
True because of the way the world must be, not merely because we happen to find it true.

questions_to_think_about: Could a name keep referring to the same person even if that person looked very different?
Is “the tallest student” a rigid designator? Why might the answer be no?
Can we learn something by observation even if it could not have been false?
When you say “you,” what keeps that word connected to the same person?

summaries.example: Suppose astronomers use “Hesperus” for the object seen in the evening and “Phosphorus” for the object seen in the morning. They later discover that both names refer to Venus. The identity “Hesperus = Phosphorus” is therefore learned empirically, or a posteriori. Yet if both names rigidly designate Venus, then the identity is necessary in the relevant, weak sense: in every possible world containing Venus, both names still designate Venus. By contrast, “Hesperus = the brightest non-lunar object in the evening sky” is contingent, since another object could have been brightest in that situation.
summaries.summary: The entry analyzes rigid designation, the view that an expression keeps designating the same object across relevant possible worlds. Proper names are the standard case, while ordinary definite descriptions are usually non-rigid because their descriptive conditions can be satisfied by different objects in different worlds. This distinction explains why an identity such as “Hesperus = Phosphorus” may be necessary if true even though its truth was discovered empirically. The entry also separates rigidity from direct reference, causal theories of reference, and descriptivism: these theories concern how expressions convey content or acquire reference, whereas rigidity concerns how designation behaves under modal evaluation. Further issues arise when rigidity is extended to indexicals, natural-kind terms, properties, general terms, and times. The view is connected with transworld identity and opposed by counterpart theories, which interpret modal claims through similar objects rather than identity across worlds. Rigidity is used in debates about theoretical identities, the necessary a posteriori, the contingent a priori, and mind-brain identity, but its scope remains contested.
key_ideas: Rigidity is primarily a semantic notion about designation, not simply another name for direct reference, causal reference, or descriptivism.
If two rigid designators refer to the same object, their true identity statement is necessary in the relevant sense, even when its truth is discovered a posteriori.
A rigid expression need not be a bare name: some descriptions can be rigid de facto because their descriptive conditions select the same thing in every possible world.
The entry distinguishes alethic rigidity from related ideas such as temporal or epistemic rigidity.
Counterpart theorists reject or revise the idea that an individual itself appears in other possible worlds, instead using similar counterparts.
Applying rigidity to natural-kind and property terms creates further disputes about abstract objects, general terms, and whether sameness of meaning is being confused with sameness of designation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Rigidity links philosophy of language with metaphysics and epistemology. It helps explain how a statement can be necessary although discovered by observation, and it supports arguments about scientific identities such as water and H2O or about whether mental events are brain events. At the same time, the theory does not settle every issue about reference: a term may be rigid without being directly or causally referential, and disagreement continues over kinds, properties, descriptions, and counterpart semantics.

important_terms.definition: An expression that refers to an object, kind, property, or other item.
An expression that designates the same object in every possible world in which that object exists, and nothing else.
A way a world or situation might have been, used in evaluating counterfactual claims.
A form of necessity concerning what is true across possible worlds; the entry mainly uses a weak version tied to worlds where the relevant object exists.
Knowable through experience or observation rather than independently of experience.
Knowable independently of experience, at least in the relevant philosophical sense.
The view that modal claims concern sufficiently similar objects in other possible worlds rather than the very same object.
The claim that an individual picked out by a rigid name is the same individual across the possible worlds being considered.

questions_to_think_about: Does the discovery that Hesperus and Phosphorus are the same object show that the identity is contingent, or only that it was difficult to know?
Can a description be rigid even though descriptions usually vary from world to world?
Does counterpart theory preserve what ordinary speakers mean by “I could have done otherwise”?
Should “water” and “gold” be treated like names of objects, or does their use require a different account?
Would a theory of direct reference by itself explain rigidity?

summaries.example: Your school might give one student two nicknames: “Captain” because of a role in a play and “Maya” as her ordinary name. If the play role later belongs to someone else, “Captain” can point to a different person in another situation. But “Maya,” when used as her name, is meant to keep pointing to Maya even when we imagine her choosing a different hobby or living in another city. This illustrates why names are often called rigid while descriptions tied to temporary roles are often non-rigid.
summaries.summary: Rigid designation is a theory about how words refer when we compare the actual world with possible alternatives. A rigid designator keeps referring to the same object in every possible world where that object exists. Proper names are the main example. Ordinary descriptions are often non-rigid because a different object could fit the description in another situation. This explains the famous case of two names for Venus: people discovered through observation that the names referred to the same planet, but if both names are rigid, the true identity between them is necessary rather than accidental. The entry stresses that rigidity is different from direct reference, causal theories of reference, and descriptivism. It also explores whether indexicals, demonstratives, natural-kind words, property terms, and general terms can be rigid. Some philosophers accept transworld identity, while counterpart theorists say modal claims concern similar objects in other worlds. Similar questions arise when we talk about the same person at different times.
key_ideas: The same object can have different properties in different possible worlds, while a rigid name still refers to that object.
A description usually follows whoever fits the description, so its reference may change.
The identity of Venus under its two traditional names was discovered by observation, yet the identity is treated as necessary if the names are rigid.
Rigidity is not identical to the theory that names refer directly, nor to the theory that names get their reference through a causal chain.
Philosophers debate whether words such as “water,” “red,” “you,” and “that flower” have rigid uses.
The idea can also be applied to time: a name may continue to refer to the same individual when we discuss different times.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction between rigid and non-rigid designators changes how we understand identity statements and “could have been” claims. It is important in philosophy of language, metaphysics, science, and philosophy of mind. It also shows why the way we discover a truth is not always the same as the way that truth holds across possible situations. Because expressions and theories differ, the entry presents rigidity as powerful but not automatically decisive in every debate.

important_terms.definition: A word or phrase that picks out something, such as a person, object, kind, or property.
A designator that continues to pick out the same object across possible situations where that object exists.
A description that can pick out different objects in different possible situations.
A way the world might have been, used when asking “What if things had happened differently?”
True in every relevant possible situation, not merely true by accident.
A theory saying that other possible worlds contain similar counterparts of us, rather than us literally existing in those worlds.

questions_to_think_about: Would “the student at the door” refer to the same person in every possible situation?
Why might learning an identity through observation not make the identity merely accidental?
If a counterpart is very similar to you but is not you, does a claim about what you could have done describe that counterpart?
Can a description such as “the successor of 2” be rigid even though it begins with “the”?
Should “water” refer to one kind in every possible world, or is that too strong?
